doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Singing and the Nat Cole discovery
title: Starting to sing and discovering Nat King Cole
summary: Singing in college, a Dick Haymes-style friend, then Bucky singing him the Nat Cole Trio records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Wow. Did use of your vocal thing come along naturally. I know I’ve been reading about Nat King Cole who — it was suggested to him like, you need to start singing, or could you, and from there, it’s history.

Well I played in I think it was the beginning of college. Since I was already singing and playing in rock bands through high school, when I went to college I had my guitar and I had with me the Kenny Rankin album, I had some Michael Franks records, and some James Taylor stuff. And I had seen guys who sat and played the guitar, you know, folk guys. And so I learned some of these Kenny Rankin songs, like “Haven’t We Met” and he did “Here’s that Rainy Day,” and he did “Sunny Gets Blue” on this one record. And then I learned some Michael Franks songs. And when I came home from college in 1980, this kid I went to high school with sang like Dick Haymes, and he looked like Dick Haymes. And his father found my father and he said, “my kid’s gotta be with your kid” they gotta put them together. And he got us a gig in his favorite restaurant in Tappan, New York on a Monday night, sitting in the corner, he bought the kid a PA and a mic and he basically got me. So for eighty bucks, forty apiece, we sat in the corner and he sang all the Dick Haymes and Sinatra songs, and we would have a little rehearsal and I’d play seven string and accompany him, and then he’d say, “okay sing something.” And I’d sing “Popsickle Toes” or “Here’s That Rainy Day.” And his sister, this is the official story now, you’re the only one, I’ve got time right, all right, his sister had a record of a guy named Frank Weber, it was of pop songs, good pop songs. And one of the songs Frank Weber covered was “Straighten Up and Fly Right.” And she said, “oh you should do this tune.” So I learned it off the Frank Weber record and I played it for my father. And he said, “that’s the old Nat Cole song. Jeez, “he said, you’ve got to get all his stuff, they’re perfect songs for you.” Because I wasn’t singing “Night and Day.” So at that very time, I know it sounds goofy, but I found Capitol records releases “The Best of the Nat King Cole Trio” Part one and two. And I go my God, boom. I walk home, I’ll never forget it, gray sky, it was like January, I said, “I’ve got ‘em.” He said, “put ‘em on, sit down.” “Paper Moon” was the first one. And he sat there and he almost sang the entire record. My father sang the whole record to me. He was singing [scats] the whole record, right down. “All right, put on ‘Body and Soul.’” “Body and Soul,” sang the entire Oscar Moore chorus to me. And then, “Here comes, listen when Nat goes” [scats], and my eyes were like this. And then I heard all that “Sweet Lorraine” “Baby, Baby All the Time,” “Gee Baby Ain’t I Good to You,” I learned all the songs. And I said now that, that’s music. That’s something I can do. It’s all there. Great jazz, the songs are singable, and I just wrapped myself around that. I’ve got to get me more of that stuff.
